title: Past perfect
tagline: Two events in the past — had + past participle shows which one really came first.
why: A good B1 story doesn't tell events in a flat line — it explains what had already happened before the main action, and that needs had + past participle. Reading Part 6 often tests the h in had as one of its missing grammar words, and examiners in Writing Part 2 reward a story where the order of events is completely clear, even when you don't tell them in the order they happened.

hook.text: Mateo: “We got to the hotel, but the room had already been given to someone else!” Sofia: “Had your parents booked it?” Mateo: “Yes, days before — the hotel had already sold it twice!”
hook.ask: Two things happened before Mateo's family arrived at the hotel. Find the verb forms with had + past participle — why do they come before the simple past arrived?

diagrams.title: Which event came first?

marks.label: the hotel had already given the room away
the family arrived at the hotel
marks.sub: past simple — the main story moment

arrows: the earlier event explains the later one
diagrams.caption: Had + past participle sends an action back before the main past-tense moment of the story.

diagrams.title: Build the sentence

sentences.note: whole sentence — earlier action (had sold) + later action (arrived)

diagrams.caption: Had/hadn't works exactly like did/didn't, but it points to an even earlier past moment.

rows.label: Structure
cells: events told in the order they happened
either order is possible — had shows which came first

rows.label: In story order
cells: We arrived. Then we found the room was gone.
We arrived, but they had already given the room away.

rows.label: Reordered
cells: not possible without confusing the reader
They had already given the room away by the time we arrived.

rows.label: Signal words
cells: already, just, never, by the time, before, after

use.point: Past perfect for the earlier of two past actions

examples.text: When we arrived, the film had already started.
Mateo had already eaten before his sister got home.
By the time the bus came, we had waited for half an hour.
examples.note: the waiting started before the bus came

use.point: before / after / by the time / when

examples.text: Sofia had finished her homework before dinner started.
After Miss Vega had checked the tickets, the bus left.
By the time we reached the hotel, the sun had already set.
examples.note: by the time = not later than this moment

use.point: already, just and never with the past perfect

examples.text: We had just sat down when the waiter arrived.
examples.note: just = a very short time before

examples.text: Nadia had never visited Cusco before that trip.
examples.note: never = not once, up to that past moment

examples.text: They had already sold our room twice by the time we arrived!

use.point: The story order and the sentence order don't have to match

examples.text: They had given the room away, so the family had to wait.
examples.note: the past perfect can come first in the sentence too

examples.text: The receptionist apologised because she had made a mistake.
examples.note: the earlier cause is explained after the later result

watch_out.wrong: When we arrived, the film already started.
watch_out.right: When we arrived, the film had already started.
watch_out.why: The earlier of two past events needs had + past participle, not the simple past.

watch_out.wrong: We had arrived, and then we had eaten.
watch_out.why: Two events in normal story order just need the past simple — save had for the one that comes first when the sentence order is reversed.

watch_out.wrong: Before I have finished, she left.
watch_out.why: Had, not have, goes with a past time reference like before I finished.

watch_out.wrong: By the time we arrive, they had left.
watch_out.right: By the time we arrived, they had left.
watch_out.why: Both halves need a past form — the later event is past simple, the earlier one is past perfect.

watch_out.wrong: Had you ever went to Cusco before?
watch_out.why: After had, use the past participle (been), not the simple past (went).

watch_out.wrong: She had saw the message before she called.
watch_out.right: She had seen the message before she called.
watch_out.why: See → seen for the participle; saw is only the simple past form.

l1.es: Cuando llegamos, la película ya había empezado.
l1.wrong: When we arrived, the film already started.
l1.right: When we arrived, the film had already started.
l1.why: Spanish había + participio matches English had + past participle exactly — use it for the earlier event.

l1.wrong: I never was in Cusco before.
l1.why: Never + a past experience before another past moment needs the past perfect, not the simple past.

l1.es: Antes de que llegara, ya se habían ido.
l1.wrong: Before I arrived, they already left.
l1.why: The event that finished earlier keeps had, even though the sentence starts with before.

l1.es: Recién habíamos llegado cuando empezó a llover.
l1.wrong: We just arrived when it started to rain.
l1.right: We'd just arrived when it started to rain.
l1.why: Recién + pluscuamperfecto = just + had + past participle for the action that finished a moment before.

remember.trick: The earlier event gets HAD — the later one doesn't!
remember.tip: Ask: which happened first? That one takes had + past participle; the second one stays in the simple past.

dialogue.title: The room that wasn't there
dialogue.context: Mateo tells Sofia, Liam and Nadia about a problem on his family's weekend trip to Cusco.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: You won't believe it — we got to the hotel, and they had given our room to someone else!

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Yes, days before! But someone had cancelled, and the hotel had already sold it again.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: So what had happened by the time you arrived?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: They gave us a smaller room instead, because they hadn't checked properly.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Had you eaten before you got there? You must have been exhausted.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: We had just eaten at a stop on the way, so it wasn't too bad.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: By the time you found a solution, had it got dark?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Yes — the sun had already set an hour before.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: At least your parents had brought warm jackets!

items.sentence: When we arrived, the film ___ already started.
items.why: the earlier of two past events

items.sentence: ___ you ever been to Cusco before that trip?
items.why: a past experience before another past moment

items.sentence: By the time the bus came, we ___ waited for half an hour.
items.why: the waiting started before the bus arrived

items.sentence: She ___ seen the message before she called.
We ___ just sat down when the waiter arrived.
items.why: just + had + participle for a moment before

items.sentence: Nadia ___ never visited Cusco before that trip.

had, not have, with a past time reference

items.why: question form of the past perfect

can_do: I can say which of two past events happened first, using had + past participle.
I can use before, after, by the time and when to link the two events clearly.
I can use already, just and never with the past perfect to add detail to a story.
summary: Past perfect = had + past participle, for the event that happened before another past event.
The later event in the story stays in the past simple.
Before, after, by the time and when link the two events and show their real order.
Already, just and never add detail to the earlier event.
The sentence order can be different from the story order — had shows which one really came first.
